responses.content:
Penicillin was discovered by Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928. Fleming was a biologist, pharmacologist, and botanist who had set up his own laboratory at St Mary's Hospital Medical School in London.

On September 3, 1928, Fleming returned to his lab after a two-week vacation to find that one of his bacterial cultures had been contaminated with a mold, later identified as Penicillium notatum. To his surprise, the mold had killed off the surrounding bacteria, including Staphylococcus aureus.

Fleming isolated the substance responsible for this phenomenon and named it penicillin. However, he was unable to purify or crystallize it at the time.

It wasn't until 1941 that a team of researchers, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain at Oxford University, developed a method to mass-produce and purify penicillin, making it available for widespread use in medicine. The first human patient treated with penicillin was a police officer named Albert Alexander, who suffered from a severe streptococcal infection. He received his first dose of penicillin on February 12, 1941.

Initially, the treatment was administered intravenously over several days, and it took weeks for the full effects to be observed. Later, shorter courses of treatment were developed, making penicillin a game-changer in modern medicine.

Fleming, Florey, and Chain were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 for their discovery and development of penicillin.
